item.title: Democracy Depends on Being Able to Forgive
item.description:
Forgiveness

Democracy Depends on Being Able to Forgive

How we respond to hurt shapes our relationships—and our society’s shared future.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Letting go of resentment can change how we respond to people who hurt us.
  • Research suggests forgiveness can be strengthened through intentional practice.
  • Accountability and forgiveness can coexist without restoring a broken relationship.

In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast this month, President Trump was asked a profound question that rarely comes up in political interviews: Could he forgive his enemies? If entering heaven required him to feel love and forgiveness for James Comey or Nancy Pelosi, could he do it?

“The answer is no,” the president said. “I want to be honest, no.”

We should resist the tempting thought that only Donald Trump feels this way. We all instead need to look in the mirror: How willing are we to forgive the people we believe have done us wrong?

For most of us, grievance has a powerful pull—whether it’s rehearsing an argument or replaying a hurtful remark over and over in our heads. In psychology, we can understand forgiveness as a voluntary change in how we feel and act toward someone who’s hurt us in the past. It can loosen the hold of resentment on our attention and, in turn, help us choose how to respond in the future.

Forgiveness: Essential for Democratic Societies

These days, the word forgiveness can sound like a concept out of a Sunday school class or a therapy session. But it’s a prerequisite for a functioning democratic society.

A country needs ways to respond to wrongdoing and still leave open the possibility of a shared future. When every injury becomes a reason for retaliation, the work of governing turns into settling scores.

Here’s the thing about democracy: It’s a continuing relationship among fallible people. It depends on our ability to correct errors, acknowledge wrongdoing, and work together again. Forgiveness is a vital civic skill because democratic societies have to do more than settle who was right in the last conflict. Forgiveness makes healthy debate and cooperation possible.

I once asked the legendary Archbishop Desmond Tutu what forgiveness meant. He simply said, “It means I no longer demand payback from you.”

When he was chair of South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Tutu helped bring apartheid-era abuses to public attention. He underscored the principle that forgiveness isn’t blanket absolution. Truth, accountability, and repair can coexist with refusing permanent vengeance. In our own lives, we can forgive someone while maintaining boundaries, including choosing not to resume a relationship.

When I interviewed former Colombian president and Nobel Peace laureate Juan Manuel Santos for my book On Belonging, he recalled advice to recognise an adversary’s humanity in war and peace. His 2016 agreement with the FARC opened a path for former guerrillas to enter into democratic politics.

This month, delivering the Nelson Mandela Annual Lecture in South Africa, Santos told the story of Pastora Mira. She cared for a wounded man who then confessed to torturing and killing her son. She embraced him, saying his acceptance of responsibility had freed her from the prison of lifelong hatred. It’s a breathtaking example. Such forgiveness remains a personal choice.

Forgiveness and Political Polarization: The Canadian Example

It’s important that we avoid thinking that the psychological grip of contempt is unique to any one country. Others—including my home country of Canada—shouldn’t think they’re immune to a politics of contempt. A 2025 Angus Reid Institute–Cardus survey found 87% of Conservative supporters regarded the Liberals as a threat to Canada’s well-being. And 84% of Liberal supporters said the same of Conservatives.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt understood forgiveness as a way to release people from being bound indefinitely to what they’ve done, allowing something new to begin. For her, forgiveness was inextricably linked to respect and to what I call belonging—that we honour people’s humanity, even if we disagree with their preferences.

Earlier this month, Texans elected James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, to the U.S. Senate. He’s spoken eloquently about loving his enemies and seeing opponents as children of God. It’s a message that draws on a Christian tradition that asks us to extend the mercy we ourselves need—a tradition Martin Luther King Jr. brought into public life more than half a century ago.

Ultimately, forgiveness is a skill we can learn. In an international study of more than 4,500 adults, people given a short program to reflect on hurt and consider another person’s perspective reported greater forgiveness and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety after two weeks than those waiting to begin. The study concerned personal relationships, but it offers reason to take forgiveness seriously as something we can actively cultivate.

We can all put this into practice. Name what happened and how it honestly affected your feelings. Try to consider the other person’s perspective, and think of a time you needed forgiveness for yourself. Give yourself time and space for your feelings to change. Choosing to forgive can precede feeling the emotion of forgiveness.

Let’s face it: In failing to forgive his enemies, Donald Trump isn’t so much of an outlier. But that needs to change. To build a healthy democratic society, we can’t have permanent enemies. We have to build a future together. That work can begin in our own relationships.

item.title: Rejected for 10 Years, Then She Made History
item.description:
Resilience

Rejected for 10 Years, Then She Made History

Astronaut Peggy Whitson teaches us about persistence, rejection, and success.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Peggy Whitson was rejected by NASA for a decade before becoming one of its most accomplished astronauts.
  • High-performers approach rejection differently, and that difference may explain their success.
  • Talent, grit, and hard work may get you started, but they won't necessarily set you apart.
Peggy Whitson worked at NASA for 10 years before becoming an astronaut.
Source: Peggy Whitson, used with permission

Peggy Whitson, a biochemist, applied for 10 years to become an astronaut. Every time she applied, she was turned down. Who applies for the same job for a decade, I thought? Dr. Whitson made it very clear to me that she would become an astronaut. She realized that there was a divide between what the selection committee was looking for and what she was showing them.

Talent is important, as is grit, resilience and a strong work ethic. That’s a baseline, not a differentiator. The difference between those who succeed despite the setbacks, and sustain that success, might just be how they approach challenges.

Whitson focused her energy and talents on closing that delta to prove to the astronaut selection committee that she was worthy of their confidence and would become a great astronaut.

Control What You Can Control

Peggy Whitson was the first female commander of the International Space Station (ISS).
Source: Peggy Whitson, used with permission

When faced with a challenge, high-performers focus on what they can control. Some circumstances are simply beyond their influence. No one can control the weather or the construction noise outside a building where they’re taking an important exam. What distinguishes high-performers is their ability to double down on the variables within their control while managing their response to those beyond it. How you react to what is beyond your control might separate those who can from those who won’t.

High-performers use setbacks as data points. Each one teaches them something new. They review it with painstaking detail. NBA player Zaza Pachulia played in 1,098 basketball games over his 15-year NBA career. After each game, he told me, he would review the video of the game, not to see what he got right, but rather, what he could improve upon (watch my conversation with Zaza Pachulia). High-performers like Pachulia review the feedback and evidence and look to see how they can improve even a fraction of a percent. Compounded they know that it will have an outsized difference between their output and everyone else’s. Then they take action. In their mind, it’s not a question if they will succeed, rather they focus on how. That’s how high-performers focus on controlling what they can control.

It’s a good thing Whitson didn’t quit on her quest to become an astronaut. Eventually, she was accepted and became the first female commander of the International Space Station (ISS), a role she’s held twice. For years she held the record for spending more days in space than any American astronaut of any gender, and eventually, she was promoted to NASA’s Chief Astronaut.

The next time you are faced with a challenge, examine what needs to happen for you to meet your goal, then look at where you are now. Then figure out how to close that gap. A setback is only a failure if you let it simmer. Take control and plan your next steps.

item.title: Egg Donation: Is It Private, or a Secret?
item.description:
Infertility

Egg Donation: Is It Private, or a Secret?

The difference between privacy and secrecy, and the overlap.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Privacy and secrecy can overlap, particularly when parents fear judgment from others.
  • Research supports telling donor-conceived children about their origins early and in age-appropriate ways.
  • Children may feel burdened when they are asked to keep their conception hidden from others.
Source: AboutLife - Raev Denis/Shutterstock

When it comes to donor conception, there is an important difference between protecting your privacy and keeping a secret.

A woman I was working with recently voiced that her biggest concern about using an egg donor was disclosure. She worried about how certain family members might react. She anticipated judgment, unwanted opinions, and criticism.

She wasn't questioning whether egg donation was right for her. Rather, she was questioning who needed to know and whether that knowledge could come back to hurt her or her family.

Our work raised two important questions: Whose information is it to share? And what is the difference between privacy and secrecy?

Privacy Is Not the Same as Secrecy

These terms are often used interchangeably, but privacy and secrecy are not necessarily the same thing.

Privacy is about choosing what information to share, with whom and when. Secrecy, on the other hand, often involves deliberately withholding information, sometimes because of shame, fear, or anticipated judgment.

For example:

  • Privacy: “Our child knows how they were conceived, but we don't feel everyone else needs to know.”
  • Secrecy: “We don't want anyone to know because we're worried they might see our child or our family differently.”

When Privacy and Secrecy Overlap

Take, for example, a woman who decides not to tell her mother-in-law that she used an egg donor. Perhaps their relationship is difficult. Perhaps she knows her mother-in-law has strong opinions about what makes a family.

Naturally, she may worry that her child will be treated or seen differently. And alongside this may be a concern that her own place as a mother will somehow be questioned.

Does that mean she is keeping a secret? Perhaps. But it may also be about privacy. She may simply be sparing herself from a conversation she doesn't want or need to have. This is personal information that belongs to her, her partner and their child. It is not necessarily something the wider family needs to know.

But she may also feel that she has no choice but to hide the information because she fears how her mother-in-law might react.

This is where privacy and secrecy can overlap. She may want to keep the information private, while also feeling that she cannot safely share it. Both can be true at the same time.

And keeping something secret does not automatically mean that someone feels ashamed or that their decision is wrong.

But What About the Child?

While parents have every right to decide who knows about their fertility treatment, donor conception also involves another person: the child. And the child's relationship with this information is different. For the child, it is part of the story of how they came into the world.

Research supports telling donor-conceived children about their origins early, using age-appropriate language and making it part of their developing understanding of themselves, rather than a “one and done” significant conversation when the child is older (Ilioi et al., 2017; Duff & Goedeke, 2024). There can be something deeply reassuring about growing up with this knowledge, rather than having to make sense of it for the first time later in life.

As the child grows, the conversation also grows. Questions change, new feelings emerge, and things that seemed unimportant at five may take on a different meaning at fifteen.

When Privacy Becomes a Burden

But what happens when parents tell their child about their conception and then ask them not to tell anyone else?

Parents may have understandable reasons for wanting to keep donor conception within the immediate family. They may want to protect their child from judgment, insensitive comments, or rejection.

But imagine a child who has always known they were conceived through egg donation, yet has been told not to mention it to grandparents or friends.

Perhaps a friend asks why they don't look like their mother. The child may want to explain but hesitate, remembering that their parents don't want anyone to know. In this way they are caught between wanting to talk about themselves and worrying about upsetting their parents.

A child may also begin to wonder: Why can we talk about this at home but not outside? Is there something wrong with how I was conceived? This is where privacy may begin to feel like secrecy. Privacy gives a child a choice about what they share, while secrecy may leave them feeling responsible for keeping something hidden.

Whose Story Is It Anyway?

As children grow older, they develop their own feelings about their genetic origins. Some may want to talk openly about being donor-conceived, others may prefer privacy. What matters is that the child is gradually given the language, understanding and freedom to decide what they feel comfortable sharing.

For example, they might say, “My parents needed help from an egg donor to have me.”

Or equally, “I don't really want to talk about that.”

Both are reasonable responses. The important difference is that the choice belongs to them.

It is OK for parents and children to have different feelings about disclosure. What is important is that parents recognize their own anxieties and try not to pass them on to their child. The child should feel free to develop their own feelings about their origins, without carrying the weight of their parents' worries.

This can be a complex challenge for parents to come to terms with. And it doesn't have to be neatly resolved. It can just be.

You Cannot Control Everyone's Reaction

Not everyone will understand or approve. Some may have deeply held beliefs about genetics and family relationships. Others may ask intrusive questions or make insensitive comments. You cannot necessarily prevent those reactions, but you can decide how much access those individuals have to your private lives.

Depending on your family and community, it may also be important to prepare your child for the fact that people have different ideas about what makes a family. Not everyone will agree with your views, and they don't have to. This too is part of diversity. There are many different ways to be human.

item.title: The Power of Kindness in a World Driven by Probability
item.description:
Relationships

The Power of Kindness in a World Driven by Probability

Personal Perspective: An antidote to probability’s search for absolute outcomes.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Probability's quest for certainty can fragment human experience and relationships.
  • Kindness offers a holistic, ecological antidote to probability’s search for finite outcomes.
  • Acts of kindness foster well-being, trust, and emotional connection beyond calculated outcomes.

"We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable." —Maria Popova

“I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” —Lady Gaga

"The question is not: what have I achieved? But rather: who can I be when I am with you? Who can you be when you are with me?" —Nora Bateson

We live in a world, at least in our hectic Western-based culture, that is driven by probability. What is probability? How does it taste, smell, or feel? Does it just linger in our complexity, waiting for a never-achieved form? We calculate within probability both with our awareness and unawareness. It penetrates our educational, economic, political, and medical systems. It assumes that we will automatically accept models of certainty. Yet our problems still exist in the domain of probable content.

Source: Natasha Rabin, used with permission

Probability is all-powerful and designed to make you believe its outcomes are absolute. It waits for our lives to pass through it with definitive rules to fit all. However, it can never seem to guarantee success. It tries to be the basis of caution, yet it can also be the source of the other side of safety. It can, in many instances, be the origin of violence and discrimination.

Why? Probability measures the likelihood or chance that a specific event will occur. It survives on unresolved paradoxes of this or that, and that misses the yin/yang, messy/beautifulness of life in all its complexity. It can be funny, as in humor, and puzzling with choices, but when not harnessed, it feels separate and fragmented, avoiding the ecological process of how all patterns connect.

Probability vs. Kindness and Connection

Probability evades the wisdom of understanding how love, altruism, and empathy can breed kindness, which some might consider the regulating homeostasis basis of living systems. Anthropologist Gregory Bateson more than hinted at the misunderstanding of probability’s faults by suggesting that absolute outcomes hide how "Human actions involve play, context, and the probability of disaster or risk within a relationship." Probability makes us too busy to savor what happens between relationships, yet when we do, it can help us step back from absolute outcomes and certainty and find improvisational potential. When we do, with encouragement, this can create all kinds of possibilities. Maria Popova, for instance, mentions in the first stanza of her poem "The Wildest Bet Is the Winning Bet":

"You wouldn’t have bet on it,
the battered rock
orbiting a star
from the discount bin
of the universe"

Probability dissolves when you zoom outward with your personal lens and widen your perspective, making room for kindness to be born. Probability, in this case, begins to blend with how we share our possessions. It becomes an advocate for tending to others' needs, which gives ultimate meaning to who we are as humans. It becomes the terrain of kindness, the quality or state of being friendly, generous, considerate, and genuinely concerned for the well-being of others. Through kindness, we can choose to blend with the paradoxes inherent in unchecked probability to see an ecological unity in a manner felt by C.S. Lewis, who wrote in Surprised by Joy: "Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else—whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard—does the 'thrill' arise." That is the prerequisite for kindness.

Using kindness as an ecological framework supports a sense of order in contrast to probability’s search for finite answers. This demand for finitude is what excludes kindness because it depends on producing outcomes. Kindness, however, is driven by understanding the constraints and interdependency of any living system. This is why it is woven into global popular symbolism and metaphors. It is based on maintaining what may be good for humanity rather than accumulating something. It is forming a kinship based on forgiveness, not to condone past pain but to move forward with altruism and empathy. Kindness emerges in what poet Allen Ginsberg poetically called a state that "stretches thru every probability." It is the beginner's mind of temporary emptiness, which can at first seem conceptually liable, mistaken for sheer nothingness, yet is in fact the improvisational potential for possibilities of kindness.

The Importance of Kindness in Human History and Society

We must recognize this need for kindness, especially in today's struggle to accept diversity. This underscores a profound reminder, particularly useful as we celebrate Thanksgiving, that the Anglo experience in North America began as a big mistake in probability, as Garrison Keillor reminds us: "...we survived only by the kindness of strangers who had every reason to be cruel." In a quote often attributed to Mark Twain, this type of innate empathy is "...the language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see."

When the dictates of probability, with seemingly good intentions, succumb to the dark side of fragmented content in our educational systems, isolated profit-driven health mandates, and sociopolitical polarization, the antidote is massive acts of kindness. This releases feel-good neurotransmitters like dopamine, serotonin, and endorphins. It activates the brain's reward center, creating euphoria and emotional warmth. It further reduces stress by soothing the vagus nerve, which recharges and rejuvenates when it feels secure.

It is interesting how unchecked probability is the cloak of "science" that constantly tries to quantify or refute the effects of kindness, when it only needs to observe how it strengthens social bonds like a welcome adhesive. Kindness can increase trust and collaboration, and encourage greater equity in the distribution of wealth, security, and opportunity, allowing for our innate interdependency with each other and nature. Another worthwhile attribute is the resulting togetherness that correlates with lower rates of anxiety and depression. Consider this in contrast to the array of physical ailments that can occur with unchecked probability, and it's a choice worth exploring.

Prompts to Cultivate Kindness Over Probability in Daily Life

Here are some prompts to help you sustain kindness as an antidote to probability. Use them with someone else or in groups. After each response, follow up with at least five “How did that affect you?” questions and ask how you can make a difference. Then discuss using paraphrasing to provide feedback about what was heard.

  • How could you have responded differently with kindness in situations in your life when you were misunderstood?
  • In what ways have you had difficulty being heard, and how would kindness have altered that situation?
  • Can you describe a time you felt uncomfortable during an event, especially within the different institutions around you, and how acts of kindness could have made a difference?
  • How do you plan to use kindness to make a difference in your life?
  • Can you describe a grievance that lacked kindness and held you back from what you wanted to attain in life, and the context in which it occurred?
  • How do you deal with forgiveness, knowing you cannot change or minimize the past, and how do you use kindness to ease this pain?
  • Using all your senses (i.e., taste, smell, touch, sight, hearing), what is it like to be with you when you share your kindness?

item.title: Does Knowing Animals Are Smart and Sentient Reduce Harm?
item.description:
Intelligence

Does Knowing Animals Are Smart and Sentient Reduce Harm?

Animals often "lose their minds" and their cognitive capacities don't matter.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • A new book is the first to study key assumptions of animal advocates and subject them to empirical scrutiny.
  • Learning more about the inner lives of animals probably does matter, but it is complicated.
  • Intelligence raises moral concern for animals, but people may disregard such findings for animals they eat.
Source: Mark Stebnicki/Pexels

People who practice animal law depend on scholars and advocates in other fields to provide the information they need to do their important work, but does this advice really reduce or end exploitation? In their fascinating and important new book Empirical Animal Law: Testing the Assumptions of a Movement, Justin Marceau, David A. Dana, and Janice Nadler offer answers to this and other important questions by insisting that lawyers working in this field must empirically test their assumptions and learn from their mistakes.

This book should be read not only by lawyers and legal scholars but also by researchers like me. It's heartening and extremely important to see actual data about the effectiveness of research in the field of cognitive ethology, the study of animal minds, and whether or not what we learn makes a difference in the lives of the animals themselves. I remain optimistic that their detailed analyses will be a positive move for increasing animal well-being across diverse species.

Here's what Marceau had to say about this first comprehensive, data-driven account of how animal law operates in practice in which he and his co-authors call for a new empirically informed movement. This book is a gold mine of information and I couldn't agree more with what they write.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you and your colleagues write Empirical Animal Law?

Justin Marceau: It is hardly controversial to recognize that the law does a poor job of protecting the lives and interests of animals. The law allows activists who attempted to rescue beagles from cruelty to be treated as criminals, while shielding directly or through practice the very institutions that harm animals. Factory farming has increased across the U.S. in recent decades. Animals continue to be bred for our fashion, consumption, entertainment, research, and sport. And almost all of this is perfectly legal.

Much of this harm remains invisible to the public despite decades of work by activists and lawyers. For some in the movement, this means that all hope is lost. There are people out there claiming that animal protection efforts have failed. Our book is a bit more optimistic, or at least focused on what is working and what is not working.

Specifically, we are legal scholars, including Janice Nadler, a renowned social scientist, and we wanted to study the strategies and assumptions of animal advocates. What kind of assumptions are we making about how best to make progress for animals, and what could be done better? In short, we wrote the book to test the assumptions of our movement about what is working and what does not work.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

JM: It is an academic book so we expect it to be useful to researchers. But we also wrote the book in an accessible format so that it can be picked up and discussed by animal advocates and lawyers across the country. Our critiques and guidance are borne out of the more than a dozen original empirical studies we conducted for the book, and we hope that the data we share in the book will help inform the next generation of advocacy on behalf of animals.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

JM: The book has several different types of studies and analysis: (1) studies on the role of incremental reform in achieving more radical reform or animal rights; (2) factors that influence our opinions about the moral standing of animals; (3) the impacts for animals and humans of a carceral or tough-on-crime approach to animal law; (4) the role of protests in social change; (5) the theory of “winning by losing” in litigation or lawmaking; and (6) questions of who are the best messengers and what are the best messages for animal advocacy and outreach.

Source: Cambridge University Press, used with permission

We think that each of these topics and studies brings new insights into questions that the animal protection field has either ignored or taken for granted. The major theme of the book, captured by the subtitle, is: Testing the Assumptions of a Movement.

One set of studies that we think are particularly important examines the relationship between an animal’s perceived moral standing and their Intelligence, emotional intelligence, or sentience.

Animal lawyers and advocates have long assumed that the law will "follow the science.” That is to say, the law will inevitably provide more protection as we learn more about the intelligence or capabilities of animals. "Just show them more science!" it is often proclaimed.

Our studies, drawing on thousands of participants, suggest that learning more about the inner lives of animals probably does matter, but it is complicated.

Intelligence, for example, does raise moral concern for animals, but people may disregard such findings for animals they already eat, though not always, as our results for fish show. Thus, in our studies, describing pigs as highly intelligent did not significantly raise their moral standing.

Information demonstrating that an animal can feel pain, on the other hand, increased the perceived moral standing for every species we tested, including pigs and cows. And that is a pretty remarkable finding. Informing people about scientific evidence of sentience can significantly increase the animal’s perceived moral standing.

Perhaps the most intriguing finding in this section is that learning about an animal's emotional life (that the animal is loving and cooperative, and mourns its dead) may be the most powerful factor of all. In our studies, learning about the emotional lives of animals increased moral concern even for cows, an animal most people regularly eat.

The idea that animal emotions or emotional intelligence can impact or challenge our entrenched habits of consumption or compassion for animals is fascinating to us. So far as we know, we are the first to empirically test this idea and we think it deserves considerably more study.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

JM: To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive effort to take up the key assumptions of animal advocates and subject them to empirical scrutiny. We can’t wait to hear what folks think about what we have found!

MB: Are you hopeful that, as people learn which kinds of information about animals’ minds, emotions, and sentience actually shift attitudes, researchers will do more to make their work accessible to a wider audience?

JM: This is key. Our research suggests that learning about the inner lives of animals can make a difference in how people perceive animals. This means that animal protection efforts need to do more to understand the science about animal lives and to translate it into forms that are digestible to the public at large.
